notes.meaning: Many years had passed since the Lord gave Israel peace from the surrounding nations. Joshua had grown very old, probably reaching the final year of his life. Even though major warfare had ended, he knew the nation still faced great spiritual dangers ahead.

Joshua gathered the elders, tribal chiefs, judges, and officers who led the people of Israel. He spoke directly to these leaders because their example and guidance would shape how the whole nation behaved. He openly pointed out his advanced age so they would listen carefully to his final instructions.

Joshua reminded the leaders of the great victories they had witnessed with their own eyes. Instead of taking credit as their military general, he gave all the glory to the Lord who fought on their behalf. Every victory Israel enjoyed was entirely a gift of God's power and mercy.

Joshua reminded the tribes that he had already divided the land among them as their inheritance, which was their God-given family property. This territory reached from the Jordan River westward to the Mediterranean Sea, covering both defeated lands and areas where enemies still lived. The tribes were to claim all of it with confidence because God had assigned it to them.

The Lord promised to drive out the remaining pagan nations so the Israelites could move in and settle there. God had given them their current peace as a pledge that He would finish what He started. Yet enjoying this complete victory depended on their willingness to step out in faith and obey Him.

Joshua urged them to be strong and resolute in keeping everything written in the Law of Moses. They were not to stray to the right or to the left by adding human ideas or ignoring God's commands. Standing firm in God's truth requires real spiritual courage when the surrounding culture pulls in the opposite direction.

The Israelites were strictly warned never to mix socially with the idol-worshiping people who still lived among them. They were forbidden from speaking the names of false gods, swearing legal oaths by them, or bowing down to worship them. Casual friendship with idolaters would slowly drag God's people into their wicked practices.

Instead of chasing after false gods, Israel was commanded to cling closely to the Lord their God. This meant loving and serving Him with deep loyalty, like a devoted husband and wife staying faithful to one another. Joshua praised them for staying loyal since crossing the Jordan, urging them to keep that same devotion.

The Lord had cleared away powerful and terrifying nations to give Israel a home. As long as the people walked with God, no enemy had been able to stand against them. Looking back at God's past help gave them every reason to trust Him for future battles.

Joshua declared that a single Israelite warrior could chase away a thousand enemy soldiers. This great power came from the Lord who fought for them, just as He had promised, not from their own strength. When God fights for His people, human numbers and odds do not matter.

The leaders were told to be very watchful over their own hearts and make sure they loved the Lord their God. Love is the true root of all genuine obedience, not mere outward rule-keeping. If our love for God grows cold, wandering into sin is sure to follow.

Joshua warned what would happen if they turned away from God to form close ties with the surviving pagan nations. The first step was friendly mingling, which would soon lead to intermarriage and shared customs. Joining family ties with people who hated the true God would inevitably pull Israel away from Him.

If Israel compromised with those nations, God would stop driving out their enemies. Instead, those surviving peoples would become traps to ensnare them, whips across their sides, and blinding thorns in their eyes until Israel died off the land. Sins that seem harmless at first always end up bringing deep pain and destruction.

Joshua announced that he was about to die, describing death as a journey every human being must take. He called them to witness that every single good promise God made had come true without a single failure. God's perfect track record shows that He can always be trusted.

Joshua warned that just as God was faithful to bring every promised blessing, He would be equally faithful to carry out His threatened judgments. God's truthfulness guarantees both His rewards for obedience and His punishment for rebellion. If the people turned to evil, they would lose the good land God had given them.

Breaking God's covenant—His sacred agreement with Israel—by serving and bowing to other gods would provoke His burning anger. The nation would quickly perish from the fertile land they had received as a gift. Missing out on the blessings God freely gave would make their ruin all the more heartbreaking.

differ.view: Warnings of losing the land show that people can turn away and forfeit the blessings God sincerely offered them.
The warning of losing the good land emphasizes the tragedy of covenant unfaithfulness, which motivates God's people to persevere.
